executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the crisis of institutional trust in artificial intelligence — who controls it, who profits from it, and whether its stewards are honest about their intentions. The Musk v. Altman trial, covered in MIT Technology Review, crystallized this tension most sharply: both men stand accused of fundamental dishonesty in their pursuit of dominance over AGI, and the jury's verdict will carry implications far beyond a single lawsuit, effectively adjudicating which vision of AI governance — corporate nonprofit hybrid or unfettered billionaire control — the public and courts find more credible. The New York Times newsletter's report on insider trading signals on Polymarket reinforces the same anxiety from a different angle, revealing that prediction markets built on AI-adjacent information ecosystems are already being gamed by those with privileged access, suggesting that opacity and self-dealing are systemic rather than exceptional. The Economist's examination of the data center backlash adds a third dimension: even as AI's power brokers fight over who should lead the technology, communities and critics are questioning whether the infrastructure costs — environmental, economic, social — are being fairly distributed or honestly disclosed. Taken together, these stories do not merely describe a technology race; they document a legitimacy crisis in which the institutions, individuals, and markets surrounding AI are each failing, in distinct but reinforcing ways, to earn the public's trust.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

A deadly shooting at a San Diego mosque dominated Monday's news cycle. Early reports indicated a security guard had been killed at the scene [2], and by late evening authorities confirmed the death toll had risen to three, with both suspects found dead [1]. The attack unfolded over several hours before law enforcement located the perpetrators. Separately, a fast-moving wildfire in California forced immediate evacuations as crews scrambled to contain the blaze [3].

On the legal and law enforcement fronts, a federal ICE agent was charged in connection with the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant in Minnesota [4], a case that drew immediate national attention amid ongoing scrutiny of immigration enforcement conduct. In a Silicon Valley courtroom, a jury rejected Elon Musk's legal claims against OpenAI, delivering a significant defeat in his high-profile dispute with the AI company he co-founded [5].

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The third and final week of the Musk v. Altman trial centered on mutual credibility destruction, with Altman accused of lying and self-dealing while Musk was cast as a power-seeker seeking to control AGI, leaving the jury to adjudicate which narrative holds.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch summarizes courtroom reporting from MIT Technology Review journalist Michelle Kim, who covered all three weeks of the Musk v. Altman trial in person; the piece responds to the conclusion of testimony and the case's handoff to the jury.
arguments: Musk's legal team attacked Altman's integrity directly, accusing him of 'lying and self-dealing' in connection with OpenAI's contested nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, framing Altman as having enriched himself at the expense of the mission he publicly championed.

Altman's defense reframed Musk as motivated not by principle but by a desire for dominance, portraying him as 'a power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence' rather than a genuine benefactor of OpenAI's founding mission.

The trial surfaced previously unreported internal culture details — including a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk' — that illustrate the toxic interpersonal dynamics underlying the legal dispute and lend color to claims about Musk's management style and temperament.
longform.significance: The case represents the first major judicial proceeding to directly interrogate the governance and founding promises of a leading AI lab, setting a potential precedent for how nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions in AI will be scrutinized. The credibility contest between two of AI's most powerful figures — conducted in open court — is producing a public record of internal OpenAI decisions that regulators, investors, and policymakers can now cite. The jury's verdict will either validate or undermine the claim that OpenAI's structural transformation betrayed its charitable mission.
questions_raised: Whether the jury will treat Musk's stated concern about AGI safety as sincere or as litigation strategy, given that his own company xAI was found to have 'distilled OpenAI's models' — a detail surfaced in week one that cuts against his standing as a disinterested plaintiff.

What legal or regulatory consequences, if any, will follow regarding OpenAI's nonprofit status and its transition to a for-profit structure, given that the trial has now placed internal decision-making on the public record.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place competitor in foundation models, particularly in AI coding, but retains a meaningful lead in AI for science that warrants equal attention.
longform.context: Written on the eve of Google I/O 2026, this piece responds to a marked shift in the competitive AI landscape over the past year, during which Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex have overtaken Google's coding tools so decisively that DeepMind engineers reportedly sought access to Claude for their own work.
arguments: Google has fallen to 'a clear third place in the foundation model race' on the metric that now defines frontier model reputation — coding — with Claude Code and Codex 'so dramatically superior' that even internal DeepMind engineers were reportedly fighting over Claude access as recently as April 2026, making a full comeback at I/O unlikely within two days.

Science and health AI represent Google's genuine competitive advantage: as 'the only frontier AI company to have earned a Nobel Prize,' Google's 2025 releases — the AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve — demonstrate leadership that LLM-dominated AI-for-science trends have only reinforced, making any new scientific tool announcements consequential regardless of press attention.

Google faces reputational and internal political pressures that complicate its conference messaging: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, protested a DoD deal via open letter, Google signed it the next day, and Hassabis's carefully maintained image as a 'Nobel Prize-winning nerd' above industry drama will be tested by these controversies even if executives attempt to avoid them on stage.
longform.significance: This piece illuminates a bifurcated Google — dominant in scientific AI yet trailing badly in the commercially decisive coding segment — which challenges the assumption that frontier model competition is monolithic. It also raises the underexamined question of whether AI-for-science leadership translates into broader competitive relevance as coding becomes the primary benchmark. The internal employee protest over the DoD deal signals that AI governance tensions inside leading labs are intensifying, not subsiding.
questions_raised: The piece leaves unresolved whether Google's Health Coach launch represents 'appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain' or simply another competitive retreat, given that OpenAI's ChatGPT Health has already defined public expectations for LLM-based medical tools.

If coding capability has become the primary reputational metric for foundation models, can Google's scientific AI leadership — however genuine — prevent talent and enterprise customers from gravitating toward Anthropic and OpenAI, or are these effectively separate competitive arenas?
